newsitem.title: ISRAEL: After Hebron, Arafat sets sights on Jerusalem.
newsitem.headline: After Hebron, Arafat sets sights on Jerusalem.

text.p: Shortly after the PLO flag was raised in Hebron, ending 30 years of Israeli occupation in most of the West Bank city, Palestinian President Yasser Arafat set his sights on Jerusalem.

Speaking to reporters in Gaza on Friday, Arafat proposed that Jerusalem could be the capital of two states, Israel and Palestine. The future of Jerusalem has not been tackled yet in Israeli-Palestinian peace talks.
"Why not have the same capital -- as Rome?" Arafat said. "Rome is the capital of two states, the Vatican and Italy. So we can have the same capital of Israel and Palestine."
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu vowed that Jerusalem would remain Israel's capital "for eternity."
In an interview with the French daily Le Figaro to be published on Saturday, Netanyahu said: "There will never be a redeployment in Jerusalem."
Arab East Jerusalem is the last Palestinian city occupied by Israel now that its troops have left most of Hebron and handed power in the city to Arafat's police force.
Israeli soldiers remain in part of the city of 100,000 Arabs guarding an enclave of 400 Jews who live and study there.

Netanyahu's handover of Hebron represented a historic turnabout for his right-wing Likud party, which traditionally opposed giving Arabs West Bank lands it considers part of the biblical Jewish homeland.
U.S. Secretary of State Warren Christopher said Netanyahu "crossed an important threshold" by agreeing to the Hebron deal and the move was bound to improve ties with the Arab world.

In an interview with international news agencies in Washington, Christopher said now was the time for Israel to "test the willingness" of Syria to resume peace talks, despite the reluctance of Damascus to do so.
Palestinian negotiator Mahmoud Abbas said he expected Netanyahu and his party would ultimately agree to a Palestinian state.
"We are confident that at the end of those talks with the Likud we will end up with an independent Palestinian state with Arab East Jerusalem as its capital," Abbas, known as Abu Mazen, told Reuters.
Palestinians view Arab East Jerusalem as their future capital. Israel occupied East Jerusalem in the 1967 war.

In an apparent softening of his hardline position on Palestinian statehood, Netanyahu told Le Figaro: "We can consider it...But we must first define the word 'state'. We need a new model which would grant autonomy in some fields and not in others."
